question: What orientation and locator-tone requirements apply to an accessible pedestrian push button?
model_answer: Direct Answer: Each accessible pedestrian push button must have a vibrotactile arrow on the button itself that clearly indicates which crosswalk signal it actuates; the arrow must have high visual contrast and be aligned parallel to the direction of travel on the associated crosswalk. A locator tone is mandatory in the accessible pedestrian signal equipment to help pedestrians with vision disabilities find the vibrotactile arrow and the push button, although the tone may be deactivated during DONT WALK periods if a qualifying passive detection system is used. Standards (mandatory): - "To enable pedestrians with vision disabilities to distinguish and locate the appropriate push button at an accessible pedestrian signal location, and to help them align with the crosswalk, each push button shall clearly indicate by means of a vibrotactile arrow which crosswalk signal is actuated by the push button. Vibrotactile arrows shall be located on the button of the push button assembly, shall have high visual contrast (light on dark or dark on light), and shall be aligned parallel to the direction of travel on the associated crosswalk." - "A locator tone shall be incorporated into the accessible pedestrian signal equipment to help pedestrians with vision disabilities locate the vibrotactile arrow, and the associated push button if a push button is provided." Guidance (recommended): - In temporary traffic control zones, if a pushbutton is used to provide equivalent TTC information to pedestrians with vision disabilities, the pushbutton should be equipped with a locator tone to notify pedestrians with vision disabilities that a special accommodation is available and to help them locate the pushbutton. Options (permitted): - The push button locator tone may default to a deactivated mode while the steady UPRAISED HAND (symbolizing DONT WALK) indication is displayed for the associated crosswalk, provided a passive pedestrian detection system activates the locator tone at all times (other than when the audible walk indication is active) that a pedestrian is present within a 12-foot radius from the push button location; where pedestrian facilities such as sidewalks are present, the passive detection requirement may be reduced to apply only to pedestrians on those facilities within the 12-foot radius. Visual evidence: [Image 1] shows the preferred (A), acceptable (B), and less-desirable (C) push button location areas on a corner, illustrating the placement context in which the push button's vibrotactile arrow must align parallel to the associated crosswalk. [Image 2] shows typical push button locations for four curb-ramp configurations (perpendicular, parallel, shared landing, and continuous surface), indicating where buttons are placed relative to ramps and crosswalks so pedestrians can align with the crossing. Citations: - Section 4K.04 Standard §1 (p.734) - Section 4K.04 Standard §2 (p.734) - Section 4K.04 Support §3 (p.734) - Section 4K.04 Option §5 (p.734) - Section 6C.03 Guidance §8 (p.781) - Section 4K.01 Support §11 (p.731) - Figure 4I-2 (p.721) - Figure 4I-3 (p.723)
gold_answer: The push button must have a high-contrast vibrotactile arrow on the button, aligned parallel to travel on the associated crosswalk. A locator tone must be incorporated; normally it is 0.15 seconds or less and repeats at 1-second intervals when the audible walk indication is not active, subject to stated exceptions.
